steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper introducing Choice-75, a dataset about decision branching in script learning. It should motivate the task from event reasoning and script learning, explain the gap, and briefly describe the dataset and our experiments with LLMs.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- Events and their relations; why they matter for intelligent systems
- Script learning as a direction of event-centric reasoning
- Gap: scripts treated as linear; the decision branching task
- Choice-75: the dataset, its collection, and LLM experiments

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Events are the basic building blocks of the world around us, and to understand the world you need to understand how events connect with each other. For the same reason, understanding events and how they relate is critical for any intelligent system. The community has worked on reasoning about event-to-event relationships for a long time and from a lot of perspectives, for example studies in temporal relationship and in hierarchical relationship, and both of these contribute to script generation. These tasks are hard because the relations between events are often implicit and commonsense is needed to uncover them.

Script learning is an important direction of event-centric reasoning. It studies how stereotypical events unfold, and this gives us a human-centered perspective of events. The notion of scripts dates back to early work; since then researchers have explored many aspects and applications of script learning, such as narratives, news events, and instructions. Together these studies show that script learning is promising for building better intelligent systems.

- Gap + task
  - most previous work: scripts as linear developments of events
  - real world: many crossroads, next event can unfold in multiple ways; when a human is the agent they decide where the script branches
  - no benchmark yet for modeling this decision-making process
  - our task: given a scenario, pick the more reasonable of two options
  - Figure 1: no train route from major city to desert at that time -> first option (plane ticket to a major city + train to the desert) not feasible, second (plane ticket to a small city right next to the desert) preferred
- Choice-75
  - first dataset for decision branching in scripts; 75 examples, one goal + two options each
  - more than 600 scenarios, difficulty levels from human judgment, optimal choices
  - follow previous work, human-in-the-loop paradigm for challenging examples
  - SoTA LLMs (text-davinci-003, gpt-3.5-turbo): performance aligns with human difficulty levels; decent, but notable headroom in hard cases
  - hope it fuels further studies in AI-powered decision-making

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Events are the basic building blocks of the world around us, and to understand the world you need to understand how events connect with each other. For the same reason, understanding events and how they relate is critical for any intelligent system. The community has worked on reasoning about event-to-event relationships for a long time and from a lot of perspectives, for example studies in temporal relationship and in hierarchical relationship, and both of these contribute to script generation. These tasks are hard because the relations between events are often implicit and commonsense is needed to uncover them.

Script learning is an important direction of event-centric reasoning. It studies how stereotypical events unfold, and this gives us a human-centered perspective of events. The notion of scripts dates back to early work; since then researchers have explored many aspects and applications of script learning, such as narratives, news events, and instructions. Together these studies show that script learning is promising for building better intelligent systems.

However, most of the previous work in script learning only considers scripts as linear developments of events. But in the real world scripts have many crossroads, where the next event can unfold in multiple ways. When a human is the agent, they decide the direction the script branches to. There is no benchmark yet that challenges an intelligent system to model this decision-making process. So we define and study this decision branching task, which is: given a particular scenario, an intelligent system has to identify the more reasonable option among two given options. Figure 1 shows one such example. The scenario is that the person finds no train route from the major city to the desert at that time. In that case it would be obvious that the first option, purchase a plane ticket to a major city and take a train to the desert, would not be feasible, and the second one, purchase a plane ticket to a small city but right next to the desert, is the preferred answer.

We propose Choice-75, the first dataset that targets this kind of decision branching in scripts. It has 75 examples and each example has one goal and two options. We also collect more than 600 scenarios, with difficulty levels based on human judgment, and the corresponding optimal choices. For the dataset collection we follow previous work and apply the human-in-the-loop paradigm to generate challenging examples. Then we experiment with state-of-the-art (SoTA) LLMs, including text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo, and we find that the level of performance of the LLMs aligns with the difficulty levels based on human judgment. The SoTA models show decent performance, but there is still notable headroom in the hard cases. We hope our dataset will fuel further studies in AI-powered decision-making.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Events are the fundamental building blocks of the world around us. To understand the world, one has to understand the ways events connect with each other. For the same reason, understanding events and their relationship is critical for any intelligent system. Reasoning about event-to-event relationships has long been a community effort from a wide range of perspectives, including studies in temporal relationship [1,2] and hierarchical relationship [3,4], both of which contribute to script generation [5,6]. These tasks are challenging because event relations are often implicit and require commonsense to be uncovered.

As an important direction of event-centric reasoning, script learning studies how stereotypical events unfold, which gives us a human-centered perspective of events. The notion of scripts dates back to [7]; since then, researchers have explored various aspects and applications of script learning, including narratives [8], news events [9], and instructions [4]. Together these studies demonstrate that script learning is promising for building better intelligent systems.

However, most previous works in script learning only consider scripts as linear developments of events. In the real world, scripts include many crossroads where the next event can unfold in multiple ways. When a human acts as the agent, they decide the direction in which a script branches. There is not yet a benchmark that challenges an intelligent system to model such a decision-making process. Therefore, we define and study such a decision branching task: given a particular scenario, an intelligent system needs to identify the more reasonable of two given options. One such example is shown in Figure 1: given a scenario where the person finds no train route from the major city to the desert at that time, it is obvious that the first option, purchase a plane ticket to a major city and take a train to the desert, would not be feasible, and the second, purchase a plane ticket to a small city but right next to the desert, is the preferred answer.

We propose Choice-75, the first dataset targeting such decision branching in scripts, with 75 examples each with one goal and two options. Beyond that, we also collect more than 600 scenarios, with difficulty levels based on human judgment, and the corresponding optimal choices. During dataset collection, we follow [10] and apply the human-in-the-loop paradigm to generate challenging examples. We then experiment with state-of-the-art (SoTA) LLMs, including text-davinci-003 and gpt-3.5-turbo, and find that the performance of LLMs aligns with the difficulty levels based on human judgment. While these SoTA models show decent performance, there is still notable headroom in the hard cases. We hope our dataset will fuel further studies in AI-powered decision-making.
